title: A germline-transmitted photosynthetic organelle in an animal

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an animal lineage whose eggs transmit a functional photosynthetic organelle to its offspring. The organelle would divide within animal cells and persist across generations without being replenished by eating algae or acquiring plastids from the environment. Under defined growing conditions, its photosynthesis would supply most of the carbon newly incorporated into adult animal biomass.

The key transition is from retaining a borrowed chloroplast to maintaining an inherited cellular component. In the sea-slug system studied by Maeda and colleagues, animals obtain chloroplasts from food and retain them without the algal nuclei. These retained chloroplasts, called kleptoplasts, can remain functional for months, but the study describes eggs as a kleptoplast-free stage and reports that kleptoplasts had never been found in sea-slug germ cells. The proposed innovation would add reliable inheritance and sustained integration to this demonstrated capacity for temporary retention.

Conceptual distinction: an inherited whole photosynthetic alga would remain a symbiont rather than meet this record’s organelle endpoint. Likewise, a food-derived chloroplast that improves survival for one animal would not establish a reproducing animal lineage with an inherited photosynthetic organelle. The target combines cellular integration, egg transmission and substantial transfer of photosynthetically fixed carbon into the animal’s own growing tissues.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would allow an animal lineage to build substantial new biomass from inorganic carbon fixed using light, under specified conditions. This would extend animal physiology beyond the documented benefit of retaining chloroplasts during starvation: the proposed endpoint requires measurable accumulation of animal carbon, supported predominantly by photosynthesis.

Conditional scientific consequence: a reproducible laboratory lineage would make organelle integration experimentally accessible across generations. Researchers could investigate how host cells regulate organelle abundance, distribute organelles to offspring, maintain their function and integrate their products into animal metabolism. Such a system could illuminate the transition from an intracellular association to a dependable inherited cellular component.

The evolutionary classification would depend on the acquisition route. Integrating an existing algal chloroplast would not automatically create a third primary plastid origin. Maeda and colleagues distinguish primary plastid acquisition from acquisition through a eukaryotic alga, which they describe as a secondary route. Stable inheritance would represent a major advance in integration without restarting the evolutionary origin of the plastid itself.

Conditional downstream possibilities include animals with reduced dependence on dietary carbon in suitable illuminated environments. Replacing agriculture or producing photosynthetic livestock would require many additional advances. Majority contribution to newly accumulated carbon would not by itself establish adequate energy supply for every activity, independence from other nutrients, useful productivity at large body sizes or ecological viability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this proposal is stable integration across an animal’s reproductive cycle: a photosynthetic organelle must remain functional, divide within host cells, enter eggs and persist in descendants without reacquisition. The documented sea-slug association supplies a starting point for intracellular maintenance, but its food-derived plastids and reported absence from germ cells do not demonstrate this inherited system. The supplied evidence does not directly establish that all kleptoplasts are incapable of division.

Genetic and biochemical maintenance must also become dependable without a retained algal nucleus. Maeda and colleagues found no detectable algae-derived photosynthetic genes in the nuclear genome assembly of the studied slug, but that result does not show that animal genes make no contribution to plastid maintenance. They proposed that some host genes might help protect algae-derived proteins; those functions remained hypothetical. Transfer of an algal photosynthetic gene set into the animal nucleus is therefore a possible integration mechanism, not an established prerequisite or the only conceivable route.

Engineering synthesis: a successful system would need coordinated organelle replication and distribution during development, reliable delivery to the germline, sustained access to the molecules needed for maintenance and repair, and movement of fixed carbon into animal metabolism. It would also need to tolerate illumination and photosynthetic activity without unacceptable cellular damage. These are proposed functional barriers implied by the target, rather than capabilities individually tested or ruled out by the supplied study.

Measurement is a separate barrier. Prolonged survival in light can demonstrate a benefit while leaving unanswered whether photosynthesis supports net growth of animal tissues. Establishing the proposed carbon contribution requires separating newly fixed carbon in animal biomass from carbon retained in the organelles, inherited reserves and dietary inputs.

current_state.text: In their study published on 27 April 2021, Maeda and colleagues sequenced Plakobranchus ocellatus type black, abbreviated PoB, and reported no evidence of algae-derived photosynthetic genes in its nuclear genome assembly. Their searches included gene models, genomic sequence and preassembled reads, with algal positive controls. This is a scoped negative genomic finding; it does not prove absolute absence beyond the searches’ detection limits or exclude contributions from the animal’s existing genes.

The study reports that PoB obtains kleptoplasts through algal feeding and retains them for approximately 3–5 months. During starvation, mean survival was 156 days in continuous darkness and 195 days under a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle, with five animals per group and a reported p value of 0.022. These results support a light-associated survival benefit in this experimental population. The authors acknowledged the absence of a plastid-free PoB control, and the experiment did not establish photosynthesis-supported accumulation of new adult animal biomass.

The paper’s Figure 1A legend reports that kleptoplasts had never been found in sea-slug germ cells, and its analysis treats PoB eggs as a kleptoplast-free stage. Together with acquisition through feeding, these observations distinguish the studied long-term kleptoplasty from the proposed egg-transmitted organelle. Earlier apparently conflicting survival findings discussed in the review concern other members of the species complex; they do not by themselves negate this result or justify generalizing it to every sacoglossan slug.

The supplied review assessed identified article and PDF extracts of the Maeda study, rather than complete untruncated documents. The main extracts ended during the references, after the passages supporting the results described here. A separate figures extraction was also truncated and contained garbled graphical labels; the germ-cell statement was available as legend text and did not depend on interpreting those labels.

The research also cites Stephens and colleagues’ 2021 article, Why is primary endosymbiosis so rare?, for a count of two primary plastid origins and an approximately 120-million-year age for the Paulinella event. No captured text from that article was available to the supplied review, so those historical details remain unverified here. That access limitation does not establish that the assertions are false.

The supplied materials establish the dated sea-slug findings but contain no retained freshness search establishing the field’s worldwide status as of November 1, 2026. They therefore neither demonstrate achievement of the proposed animal organelle nor justify a universal claim that no animal lineage has achieved it by that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed inheritance demonstration: maintain an animal lineage for at least five generations in which a photosynthetic organelle passes through eggs without renewed acquisition of algae or plastids from food or the environment. Track the organelle through eggs, embryonic development and adult tissues, and demonstrate its division within host cells. Five generations is an operational threshold proposed for this record, not an established biological definition or consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Egg-transmitted organelles divide without reacquisition for at least five generations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed integration demonstration: exclude the persistence of a whole algal symbiont and establish sustained organelle function supported within the animal. Cellular, molecular and physiological evidence should explain how the organelle is maintained and inherited. A transferred algal gene set should not be mandatory if another mechanism convincingly supplies the required support. The study’s combination of plastid retention without algal nuclei and no detected photosynthetic gene transfer makes this distinction particularly relevant.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained organelle function receives animal support without whole-algal symbionts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed carbon demonstration: under a stated light regime and growth interval, isotope tracing combined with carbon accounting should show that photosynthetically fixed inorganic carbon supplies more than half of newly accumulated adult animal carbon biomass. The denominator should exclude organelle biomass and inherited carbon stores. Controls should distinguish dietary carbon, environmental inputs, redistribution of existing reserves and net tissue growth. The majority-carbon threshold is a proposed performance target, not a published standard.
completion_criteria.label: Photosynthesis supplies over half of newly accumulated adult animal carbon

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat inheritance and carbon-contribution measurements across independent lineages and experimental runs, with independent laboratory replication providing stronger confirmation. Report light intensity and schedule, temperature, nutrient supply, growth, survival and fertility, including conditions under which the system fails. A finite demonstration would establish performance across the tested generations and conditions, rather than indefinite stability or universal performance in animals.
completion_criteria.label: Inheritance and carbon contributions reproduce with reported practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Longer survival during starvation alone would not satisfy these criteria, because it does not demonstrate egg transmission, organelle division or majority support of new animal carbon. An association requiring renewed symbiont acquisition would fail the inheritance criterion; even inherited whole algae would require a separate distinction from the organelle endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Starvation survival and whole-algal inheritance alone are insufficient

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—ZOO-01, A fertile animal booted from a chemically synthesized genome, overlaps through the challenge of coordinating cellular functions into a reproducing animal. Its endpoint concerns the synthetic origin of the animal genome; ZOO-06 concerns an inherited photosynthetic compartment and its metabolic contribution. ZOO-09, A heritable body plan the ancestor never had, shares the requirement for a stable inherited novelty, but photosynthetic integration need not create a new body plan.

Roster comparison—ZOO-08, Experimental origin of animal multicellular development, intersects with organelle allocation during development, but asks how animal multicellularity originates rather than how an existing animal incorporates photosynthesis. ZOO-10, Fertile adulthood from a vertebrate cell line, with no gestational parent, concerns development and reproduction outside the usual gestational route; success would not itself establish a photosynthetic organelle or carbon autonomy.

Roster comparison—ZOO-02, Complete limb regeneration in an adult mammal, concerns rebuilding complex anatomy. ZOO-03, Negligible senescence as an installed life-history program, concerns sustained organismal maintenance over time. Both could intersect with metabolic engineering, but neither follows from photosynthetic carbon supply, and neither is a prerequisite for the inheritance capability defined here.

Roster comparison—ZOO-04, Self-sustaining populations reconstructed from extinct animal species, shares the need to establish reproduction and persistence across generations, while targeting restoration of an extinct lineage. ZOO-05, Two-way semantic communication with another animal species, concerns communication and cognition rather than intracellular inheritance. ZOO-07, Reversible whole-animal biostasis, concerns recovery after a suspended state rather than sustained photosynthetic growth. Each remains a distinct innovation.

The closest mechanistic connections are to kleptoplasty, endosymbiosis and organelle evolution. Kleptoplasty demonstrates retention of acquired plastids; the target adds stable inheritance and sustained functional integration. Acquisition through a eukaryotic alga also connects the proposal to secondary plastid acquisition, while preserving the distinction from a new primary plastid origin.

change_log.change: Preserved ZOO-06’s identity and combined egg transmission, intracellular division, functional integration and majority contribution to new adult animal carbon into a single explicit target.
change_log.reason: These capabilities jointly distinguish the proposed innovation from temporary plastid retention.

change_log.change: Removed the asserted automatic consequence of a third primary plastid origin and explained acquisition-route classification.
change_log.reason: Integration of an existing algal chloroplast does not create a new primary origin; the reviewed source distinguishes secondary acquisition through a eukaryotic alga.

change_log.change: Scoped the genomic and inheritance findings to the studied system and removed the implied demonstration that all kleptoplasts fail to divide.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports food acquisition, reported germ-cell absence and negative genomic searches, but does not establish universal division failure.

change_log.change: Replaced obligatory algal gene transfer with a requirement for demonstrated functional support, retaining the possibility of host-gene contributions.
change_log.reason: Absence of detected algal photosynthetic genes does not exclude animal genetic support; proposed protective host-gene functions remained hypothetical.

change_log.change: Added the 2021 experiment’s organism designation, retention interval, survival means, light schedule, sample size, reported p value and control limitation.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the demonstrated achievement while bounding its interpretation and distinguishing survival from net biomass production.

change_log.change: Retained the historical primary-origin assertions as explicitly unverified attributed material and bounded present-day coverage.
change_log.reason: The Stephens article had no captured text for review, and no retained freshness search established worldwide status in 2026.

change_log.change: Clarified proposed completion thresholds, carbon accounting, exclusion of whole algal symbionts, reproducibility and environmental boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original thresholds were useful proposals but needed a defined biomass denominator and safeguards against mistaking retained carbon or starvation survival for new animal growth.

change_log.change: Added comparisons with every other supplied roster entry while keeping their endpoints distinct.
change_log.reason: Shared developmental, metabolic or inheritance challenges do not make the innovations interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any animal lineage had achieved the full proposed capability by November 1, 2026.
The Stephens article’s primary-origin count and approximately 120-million-year Paulinella date remain unverified because its text was not captured for review.

The mechanism sufficient for stable organelle maintenance and egg transmission remains unspecified; the reviewed evidence neither establishes obligatory algal gene transfer nor validates the proposed protective functions of host genes.
The reviewed evidence does not directly resolve kleptoplast division capacity across the relevant organisms.
The PoB survival experiment lacked a plastid-free PoB control and does not establish the fraction of newly accumulated animal carbon supplied by photosynthesis.
Five generations and a greater-than-half carbon contribution remain proposed operational thresholds; their sufficiency for demonstrating practical long-term stability has not been established.

brief.title: Animals that inherit the ability to grow using light
possible: Animals could grow new tissue using light and pass that ability to their offspring through eggs. An organelle, a working component inside a cell, would perform photosynthesis: using light to make material for growth. It would supply most of the carbon added to adult tissues without repeated meals of algae.
why: Such animals could depend less on food for the carbon they need to grow. Researchers could also study, across generations, how an animal maintains a new cellular component, passes it to offspring and uses what it produces.

sources.showed: This review examines why the acquisition of photosynthetic cell components from engulfed organisms is rare.
sources.cited_for: It provides evolutionary background on the origins of photosynthetic cell components.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an animal with an inherited photosynthetic organelle.

sources.who: Taro Maeda, Shuji Shigenobu and colleagues
sources.showed: They found no detectable algae-derived photosynthetic genes in the studied sea slug's nuclear genome, its main store of genetic instructions. Light prolonged survival during starvation.
sources.quote:
Nevertheless, it was confirmed that light
illumination prolongs the life of mollusk under starvation.
sources.cited_for: The work shows that borrowed photosynthetic components can benefit an animal without detectable transfer of algal photosynthetic genes.
sources.not_established: The small survival trial lacked a control slug without these components and did not demonstrate inherited organelles or new tissue growth.

shown: Maeda and colleagues studied sea slugs that retain chloroplasts, the photosynthetic components of algae, for months after eating them. The retained components function without the algae's nuclei, which hold most of their genetic instructions. The slugs' eggs lack these borrowed components.
missing: A lineage still needs to demonstrate organelle division inside animal cells and reliable passage through eggs without reacquisition.
The animal must sustain and repair the organelle without keeping a whole alga alive inside it.
Measurements must establish how much newly grown animal tissue comes from photosynthesis, excluding organelle material, inherited stores and food.

milestones.label: Egg transmission and division persist for five generations
milestones.explanation: Organelles would have to pass through eggs, divide inside animal cells and persist without reacquisition for at least five generations. This would demonstrate inheritance across the reproductive cycle.

milestones.label: The animal sustains organelles without whole algae
milestones.explanation: Evidence would have to explain how the animal maintains functioning organelles without whole algae living inside it. This would establish cellular integration, whether or not algal genes have transferred.

milestones.label: Photosynthesis supplies most new adult tissue carbon
milestones.explanation: Carbon tracing would have to attribute over half of newly accumulated adult animal carbon to photosynthesis, excluding organelles and inherited stores. This would establish a contribution to growth.

milestones.label: Inheritance and growth results repeat within defined conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent lineages and repeated experiments would have to reproduce inheritance and carbon contributions, with growing conditions and failures reported. This would establish reliability and practical limits.

milestones.label: Survival benefits and inherited whole algae remain insufficient
milestones.explanation: Longer starvation survival or inherited whole algae alone would not qualify, and renewed acquisition would fail inheritance. The result must meet the organelle, division and new-carbon requirements together.

uncertain: The mechanism that could sustain organelles and deliver them into eggs remains unresolved; transfer of algal genes may not be necessary.
Whether borrowed chloroplasts can divide across the relevant animals remains unresolved.
The proposed inheritance duration and majority-carbon target may not be sufficient to establish long-term stability.

page.title: Germline inheritance of photosynthetic plastids in animals
page.definition: An animal lineage maintains plastids—photosynthetic cellular compartments—that divide inside animal cells and pass through eggs without renewed uptake from food or the environment. The plastids use light to fix inorganic carbon and supply carbon compounds to the animal without retaining an algal nucleus.

goal.need: In Plakobranchus ocellatus type black, mean starvation survival was 195 days under a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle versus 156 days in darkness, with 5 animals per group and p=0.022. Transplanted chloroplasts in cultured hamster cells retained photosystem II activity for at least 2 days. These results establish a physiological benefit and intracellular photochemistry, respectively; neither establishes an inherited source of photosynthetic carbon.

figures.caption: Starvation survival of Plakobranchus ocellatus type black, reported on 27 April 2021.
figures.note: The experiment lacked a plastid-free control of the same animal.

statements.quote: Transmission to the germline remains a final barrier towards a more permanent photosynthetic animal.
statements.context: The review appeared online on 22 December 2010 and in the issue dated 15 January 2011. Germline transmission means passage through cells that produce eggs or sperm.

completion.title: An animal lineage repeatedly transmits functional photosynthetic plastids through eggs without reacquisition.
completion.criterion: A reproducing animal lineage maintains plastids that grow and divide inside animal cells, retain carbon-fixing photosynthesis, and supply fixed carbon to animal tissues. The plastids pass through eggs into reproductive offspring, and transmission recurs in descendants without renewed acquisition of algae or plastids. Cellular evidence excludes a retained algal nucleus and establishes host-supported maintenance of the photosynthetic compartment.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion, drawing on published plastid-integration hallmarks and the germline barrier identified by Rumpho et al.; no external animal-specific completion standard was located.
completion.basis: Searches of JST/JSPS programme records, developer statements, standards and prize criteria, and organelle-integration literature found no animal germline completion standard. The test combines cellular and metabolic integration with the published germline objective. No fixed generation count or biomass-carbon percentage is imposed. The cited animal results do not satisfy this combination.

milestones.title: Plastids inside animal cells perform photosystem II electron transport.
milestones.criterion: Intracellular plastids exhibit photosystem II electron transport, measured by light-dependent chlorophyll fluorescence, with microscopy establishing their location inside animal cells. Aoki et al., published online on 31 October 2024, detected activity 2 days after chloroplast incorporation in CHO-K1 hamster cells; Figure 6 reports 6 imaging regions at that time. This establishes photochemistry, rather than carbon fixation or inheritance.
milestones.set_by: Chloroplast-transplantation and kleptoplasty research convention: chlorophyll fluorometry tests functional photochemistry, as applied by Aoki et al. and described by Christa et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: the electron transport system remained active for at least 2 days.

milestones.title: An animal retains functional chloroplasts for over 20 days during starvation.
milestones.criterion: Chloroplasts remain photosynthetically functional for over 20 days during starvation, meeting the cited long-term-retention classification. Maeda et al., published on 27 April 2021, measured photosystem II maximum quantum yields of 0.57–0.64 after 109–110 days in Plakobranchus ocellatus type black, with 3 animals in that group. Maintenance used a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle and illumination of 10 µmol photons m−2 s−1.
milestones.set_by: Sacoglossan kleptoplasty classification, attributed to Händeler et al. and explicitly stated by Christa et al. (2014); published for sea slugs.
milestones.threshold_quote: those incorporating functional chloroplasts for over 20 days during starvation are called long-term-retention forms (LtR).

milestones.title: Photosynthetically fixed inorganic carbon enters plastid-free animal tissues.
milestones.criterion: Isotope tracing demonstrates light-dependent transfer of bicarbonate carbon into plastid-free animal tissues, with dark and unlabeled controls. Cruz et al., published on 29 June 2020, detected 13C labeling in Elysia viridis albumin glands after 3 hours. Imaging sampled 3 animals at each of 1.5, 3, 6 and 12 hours; incubations used 3 independent containers per treatment. This supports photosynthate transfer without establishing its fraction of newly accumulated animal biomass.
milestones.set_by: Kleptoplasty research convention: isotope-traced transfer into plastid-free host tissues, applied by Cruz et al. (2020) and earlier radiocarbon studies discussed in that paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: followed by a rapid accumulation into chloroplast-free organs.

milestones.title: Animal cells propagate functional plastids through cell division without reacquisition.
milestones.criterion: A plastid population grows, divides and passes to daughter animal cells during host-cell proliferation without renewed uptake, while retaining photochemistry and carbon transfer. Stephens et al. describe coordinated host–plastid division in Paulinella, a unicellular protist. Allard et al., published online on 25 June 2025, identified host-derived kleptosomes that support ingested chloroplasts in sea slugs; that result establishes host support, rather than plastid population renewal through animal cell divisions.
milestones.set_by: Atlas operational extension of the Paulinella cellular-integration example in Stephens et al.; searches of animal chloroplast-transplantation studies and organelle-integration literature found no published animal-specific somatic-propagation checkpoint.

not_found: No external completion standard for germline-transmitted photosynthetic plastids in animals was found in programme records, developer statements, standards, prize criteria or organelle-integration literature.
No externally set five-generation minimum or majority contribution to newly accumulated animal biomass carbon was found.
No published animal demonstration combining plastid population renewal through host-cell division with recurrent egg transmission was found.
